CITE: objective_context
ASSUMPTION: Scope note: the attached assumption pools are mixed across candidates (the QO and NPB/KBO candidates carry coaching, rain-delay and draft assumptions). Each candidate below is judged only on its own IDEA text.

ASSUMPTION: [Coaching hire] Recurrence is annual but small, at a few hires or retentions a year. Value per coach is asserted ("many players, multiple seasons") with no size supplied, so the stake is plausible but unquantified.
ASSUMPTION: [Coaching hire] The data is lawful and public (staff announcements, Statcast), but "available at decision time" fails for assistant and minor-league roles. Tenure dates are inconsistently recorded, and a coach's actual role (who worked with whom) is not public.
ASSUMPTION: [Coaching hire] Historical coach moves number perhaps in the low hundreds league-wide, but each coach touches few identifiable players. The outcome (player change) is observable, while the counterfactual is not.
ASSUMPTION: [Coaching hire] Actionability is low-to-moderate. Hires are driven by fit, cost, manager preference and availability, and a noisy rating is unlikely to override them.
ASSUMPTION: [Coaching hire] Clubs likely already evaluate coaches with private tracking data and player-development staff. Public Statcast gives only outcomes and pitch-level changes, not the coaching intervention.
ASSUMPTION: [Coaching hire] It would look useful through regression to the mean (players are hired or moved after bad years), selection (teams acquire players they expect to improve), and playing-time, park and aging confounds. Overlapping coaches make credit unassignable, and ex-post storytelling about "coach X fixed him" will match any noisy result.
ASSUMPTION: [Coaching hire] A falsifiable test is year-T-trained coach ratings predicting year T+1 player change at other clubs better than a prior-tenure reputation proxy, with out-of-time splits. A null result is the likeliest outcome and is itself informative.

ASSUMPTION: [Non-tender] The decision recurs every year for the arbitration-eligible roster, with a late-November or early-December deadline. Value per case is the projected arbitration salary minus replacement cost, which is moderate and unquantified here.
ASSUMPTION: [Non-tender] Projected arbitration salaries come from public comparables (MLBTR-style estimates), and non-tender lists are public after the deadline. The replacement market "that winter" is not known at the deadline, so the forecaster must predict who will be non-tendered league-wide, which is a hindsight trap.
ASSUMPTION: [Non-tender] The history is roughly a decade or more of non-tender classes, with a modest number of notable cases per class. Outcomes (signing price, next-season production) are observable, though only for players who signed.
ASSUMPTION: [Non-tender] Actionability is good, since the GM decides at a fixed date. The baseline (WAR per dollar against a threshold) is already a sound rule that clubs run, and the key inputs, the projection and its error, are the same ones public systems use.
ASSUMPTION: [Non-tender] It would look useful if the backtest scores only players who were actually non-tendered and later succeeded (survivorship), or compares the model with a strawman threshold instead of the club's real rule. Small annual samples and the "played in MLB last year" lesson from the prior experiment suggest a simple rule captures most of the value.

ASSUMPTION: [Qualifying offer] The decision recurs only if the club has eligible departing free agents, so expected annual value is discounted by that. The stake is the QO salary against a compensation pick, whose value depends on CBA terms not supplied.
ASSUMPTION: [Qualifying offer] Public data at decision time includes age, WAR, injury history and the QO amount. Agent and market depth are weakly public, and acceptance behavior depends on private player preferences.
ASSUMPTION: [Qualifying offer] Historical cases number perhaps a few dozen per year league-wide since 2012, which is far too few for a calibrated model with many features. Acceptance is rare and observable, but the counterfactual if a declined player had been accepted is not.
ASSUMPTION: [Qualifying offer] Actionability is clear: a binary decision within days after the World Series. The baseline (offer when expected AAV clearly exceeds the QO) is close to the optimal structure, so only borderline cases are affected, which is a handful of players per decade for one club.
ASSUMPTION: [Qualifying offer] It would look useful by overfitting dozens of cases and by describing rule changes as signal (QO amount, compensation rules and acceptance incentives shifted over time). The CBA transition may also change the QO regime, invalidating the training history.

ASSUMPTION: [NPB/KBO posting] Events are few per year and the value per signing is potentially large. The Cubs are a bidder on only a subset, so expected yearly value is lumpy and dependent on who is posted.
ASSUMPTION: [NPB/KBO posting] Public foreign-league stats are available, but the best pitch-tracking and bat-tracking data is often proprietary, so the public version of the model may be weaker than scouting. Posting windows are public only after the player is posted, and the contract price is set by competition, with a winner's-curse problem.
ASSUMPTION: [NPB/KBO posting] The number of posted players with multi-season MLB outcomes is probably a few dozen to low hundreds over the posting era, split by hitter and pitcher, with differing league environments (ball and rule changes) over time. The outcome is observable but heterogeneous.
ASSUMPTION: [NPB/KBO posting] Actionability is moderate, since the bid is the club's own decision, but the posted player's preferences, the posting fee rules and competing bids bound it.
ASSUMPTION: [NPB/KBO posting] Sophisticated clubs already run translation models and employ Asia-based scouts, and public sources (Fangraphs-style ZiPS translations) provide baselines. It would look useful when a few famous successes or busts are fitted post hoc, when the sample is dominated by stars, or when the test compares it with a naive ratio rather than with published translations.

ASSUMPTION: [Postseason roster] The decision recurs only when the club qualifies, about 1 to 4 roster sets in a qualifying year. The stake is per-series win probability, and the marginal roster slots (25th and 26th men) probably move it by a small amount, which is unquantified.
ASSUMPTION: [Postseason roster] Opponent, rotation and public splits are largely public before a series, but health and availability are not fully public at the deadline, and the managers' actual usage plan is private.
ASSUMPTION: [Postseason roster] The history is a few dozen series per year league-wide, and rosters are not randomly assigned, so the outcome (series result) is observable but swamped by game-level noise. An effect of a percentage point cannot be detected from that history.
ASSUMPTION: [Postseason roster] Actionability is decent for the final roster spots, but managers concentrate usage on the top relievers and starters regardless, and health often forces the choice.
ASSUMPTION: [Postseason roster] Contenders likely run private simulations. It would look useful through simulated gains that cannot be falsified, by scoring on the winners' rosters, or by crediting a roster with a series result that is mostly luck.

ASSUMPTION: [Arbitration filing] The decision recurs every January across the arbitration-eligible roster, and awards compound into later raises. The stake is the gap between the filing midpoints, which is typically small per player, so the total is meaningful but bounded.
ASSUMPTION: [Arbitration filing] Filing figures and hearing results are public after the exchange. The panels' reasoning and settlements are not fully recorded, and the CBA's arbitration rules may change, which would shift the process.
ASSUMPTION: [Arbitration filing] Hearings number only a handful per year league-wide (possibly single digits to low teens), so over a decade there might be on the order of 100, with a heavy dependence on a few decision panels. The outcome is observable (the club or the player wins), but only for cases that went to a hearing, which is a selected sample.
ASSUMPTION: [Arbitration filing] Actionability is high on a short timeline, but many clubs follow a file-and-trial policy that they treat as strategic rather than outcome-driven, and the settlement option constrains the filing number.
ASSUMPTION: [Arbitration filing] Clubs and outside firms already hold this knowledge, and the standard comparables rules make the midpoint baseline hard to beat. It would look useful through overfitting a small hearing set, ignoring selection into hearings, or reporting accuracy on hearing wins that the midpoint already predicts.

ASSUMPTION: Blind spot: the set is dominated by small-N annual decisions. The prior experiment's lesson, that a simple baseline captures most value, applies to most of them, so each needs a stated minimum detectable effect before building anything.
ASSUMPTION: Blind spot: a retrospective test can mislead through look-ahead on projections and through market-clearing prices that already contain the information. No candidate states a "decision-time snapshot" archive requirement, and archived projections and arbitration estimates may not exist.
ASSUMPTION: Blind spot: the candidates share a CBA-expiry dependency (arbitration, QO, service time, draft rules), so the history may stop being predictive after the next agreement.
ASSUMPTION: Blind spot: the value at stake is unquantified for all six candidates, and no ranking by expected dollars or wins per year is possible with the supplied evidence.
ASSUMPTION: Blind spot: the Cubs' internal tools are unknown, so "edge over the club's baseline" cannot be measured. The only honest comparator is a published public baseline.

IDEA: Sharpened replacement: run a pre-registered "baseline-versus-model" harness in which, for each candidate, the decision-time snapshot, the club's simple rule, a minimum detectable effect and the number of available historical cases are fixed before any model fitting. Build software only for decisions that pass (likely the non-tender and tender workflow, using frozen public projections and arbitration estimates as inputs), and treat coaching attribution as a research test whose null result would be informative.

IDEA: Coaching hire evaluation (sharpened) - build a public coach-movement ledger, but use it first as a falsification study across all 30 clubs to test whether coach-attributed player change persists year over year, and only then as a hiring screen, with a pre-registered kill criterion.
ASSUMPTION: Coaching hires recur yearly, but a club fills only a handful of major-league and upper-minors slots, so the per-club decision count is small even if league-wide history is larger.
ASSUMPTION: Public staff announcements and media guides may be incomplete or misdated for assistant and minor-league roles, so coach-to-player linkage may be wrong.
ASSUMPTION: Coach effects are confounded by roster turnover, playing time, selection of players a club expects to improve, organizational infrastructure, and regression to the mean, so unidentifiable effects are a live possibility.
ASSUMPTION: Most coaches touch few movers, so intervals may be too wide to change a hiring decision; the test is whether year-T ratings predict year T+1 better than a reputation proxy such as prior big-league tenure.
ASSUMPTION: The outcome is observable (player metrics) but the counterfactual is not, so the test is predictive, not causal.

ASSUMPTION: The decision recurs every late November and the number of borderline players per club is small, so value per year is likely modest and unquantified here.
ASSUMPTION: Projected arbitration salaries, non-tender lists and signings are public, but the replacement market is only partly known at the deadline since non-tendered players are revealed at the deadline itself; using the later list is hindsight.
